deep.reconstruction: There is no mathematics on this page. It is not a Riemann manuscript leaf. It is a printed page, p. 294, from Thomas Babington Macaulay's 'History of England from the Accession of James II', Chapter III ('State of England in 1685'), section on the navy. The running head reads 'HISTORY OF ENGLAND' and the chapter marker 'CHAP. III.' is in the margin. The neighbouring pages are the same work: p. 293 (previous) and p. 299 (next), with handwritten folio numbers '77' and '78'. This suggests loose printed leaves were filed in the 'R.Varia' bundle, either misfiled or kept by the Riemann family. The text describes the English fleet at the death of Charles II: nine first rates, fourteen second rates, thirty-nine third rates, and many smaller vessels. Macaulay says this force existed 'only on paper'. He cites Pepys's 1684 memorial to Charles II and Bonrepaux's report to Louis XIV, both describing the navy's decay. The footnote cites a despatch from Bonrepaux to Seignelay dated Feb. 8/18, 1686, an Old Style/New Style double date. Macaulay says it was transcribed for Charles James Fox from the French archives during the Peace of Amiens and later lent to him by Lady Holland and Lord Holland. There are no derivations, formulas, marginal calculations or annotations in Riemann's hand visible on the page.
errors: No mathematical content, so no mathematical errors to assess.

The catalogue attribution of this folio as a Riemann mathematical manuscript appears mistaken. It is a printed page of Macaulay's History of England (vol. I, ch. III, p. 294), unannotated as far as visible.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a printed leaf from Macaulay's History of England with no mathematical content and no visible Riemann annotations. Its only interest is archival: it shows that non-mathematical printed material ended up in the 'R.Varia' bundle.

checkable.asserts: The total number of first, second and third rates listed on the page is 62 (trivial arithmetic on the text's figures).
The double date 'Feb. 8/18, 1686' reflects the 10-day gap between the Julian (Old Style) and Gregorian (New Style) calendars in the 17th century.

transcription_corrections: The transcription of the printed text is essentially accurate. The footnote date is the dual-calendar notation 'Feb. 8/18. 1686' (a fraction-like stacked 8 over 18), not a mathematical fraction.
Unlike the neighbouring pages (handwritten '77' and '78'), no handwritten folio number is clearly visible on this page.
The next page in the bundle is printed p. 299, so printed pp. 295–298 are absent from this sequence.
